messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas, a 69‑year‑old financial analyst, remembers the day his wife, Maria, died with the same clarity that a picture frame still holds a faded portrait. The morning he was on his way to the office, she was in a car that had collided with a delivery truck, the impact instant, the world of her and Thomas snapped into stillness. Thomas has carried that image ever since: a flash of the rearview mirror, the screech of tires, the cold, silent apartment that waited for her return. He tells himself that when the memory surfaces, he feels a surge of panic, his chest tightening, the urge to retreat. It is precisely when this intrusive memory hits that Thomas’ heart pounds, he sweats, and he feels the sting of anger and guilt, emotions that flare each time he hears others talk about loss, each time a funeral flyer crosses his desk or a colleague mentions a graveyard. In those moments, the triggers—loss themes, the sudden memory of the crash, the sight of funerals or graves—activate a storm of threat, a physical reactivity that leaves him feeling hyper‑alert and on edge. The intense negative emotions that erupt when these triggers strike do more than just momentarily disturb Thomas; they sharpen his sensitivity to loss cues. After the first month of mourning, a casual conversation with a coworker about a distant relative’s funeral would set his shoulders stiffening and his eyes watering. He finds himself anticipating that anyone who mentions a funeral or death will trigger the same physical reactivity and anger he once felt at the funeral itself. This anticipation, a lingering sense of threat, makes the mere mention of loss a low‑threshold trigger, and each encounter leaves him feeling more overwhelmed than the last. To escape the weight of these feelings, Thomas has adopted a range of maladaptive strategies. He deliberately numbs his emotions, telling himself that feeling nothing is safer than feeling everything. He steers clear of any place that could remind him of Maria—he no longer attends memorial services, skips family gatherings where the word “remember” hangs in the air, and turns away from any photograph of her. He also keeps his thoughts of the crash buried deep, insisting that the more he thinks about it, the worse he will feel. Yet, the avoidance of grief reminders does the opposite of quieting the memory; it keeps the traumatic event alive in a detached, suppressed form, and each time Thomas finally encounters a funeral flyer or hears a colleague mention loss, the suppressed image erupts with even more force. His strategies of numbing and avoidance thus become catalysts that intensify the triggers, forcing him back into a cycle of distress whenever he confronts anything that might bring Maria back into his mind. The numbing and suppression themselves feed the very threat they aim to mitigate. Thomas experiences an undercurrent of irritability that often shows up in brief, sharp outbursts at work. A misaligned spreadsheet, a colleague’s offhand comment about a deceased client, or even a simple email subject line referencing a memorial can ignite his anger, turning his calm day into a series of tense, physical reactions—hands clenched, a racing heartbeat, the familiar tightening in his chest. The physical reactivity and the outbursts reinforce his belief that he cannot cope with these emotional waves, reinforcing his avoidance of grief reminders and his reliance on emotional numbing. In the quiet moments at the office, he finds himself increasingly detached from the numbers on his screen, feeling as though his focus is slipping as rapidly as his thoughts slip into the dark recesses of memory. Thomas has worked for three decades, balancing budgets and forecasting markets. Yet now, months after Maria’s death, he finds himself arriving late, leaving early, and feeling increasingly isolated. He has become less communicative with his colleagues, who begin to see him as aloof, and his performance reports show a drop in precision. He fears that if he does not change his avoidance, he might lose his job, which would add another layer of threat to his already fragile sense of security. It was this growing sense of isolation, combined with the constant physical discomfort he feels when confronted with any death‑related cue, that finally pushed Thomas to seek help. He is now ready to face the memories that haunt him, fearing that the unspoken anger and numbness that have defined his life will only continue to erode his relationships and his work. He hopes that learning to recognize the triggers before they spiral into threat will allow him to regain control, to find a steadier path through grief without losing himself in it.
